title: A Place at the Table
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 22 of 40
content:
There was an empty place at the table even when every seat was taken. The long table in the shop carried the smell of wood grain, and Ba Sing Se woke around us in cart wheels, shutters, and distant voices. I had learned that Iroh's shop was never merely a shop. It was refuge, theater, kitchen, meeting place, and sometimes a place where an old general pretended he had no past. I had also learned that pretending was different from lying. Today I wanted to know which one he asked of me.

The plan was to make the shop feel like ours without erasing who survived there before me. Iroh made difficult things sound easy because he believed they deserved a calm beginning. He poured tea, straightened a chair, and turned a practical task into a small ceremony. I let him do it for a while. Then I asked what part belonged to him and what part belonged to me. His eyebrows lifted. I had learned not to mistake that expression for surprise. Often it meant he was delighted to be challenged.

The complication was already there: Iroh kept reserving the best chair for visitors who might never return. It arrived without announcing itself, as important things often did. Iroh's posture changed first. The hand holding the cup became still. His smile remained, but it was no longer doing all the work. He served every customer with the focus of a general reading a map. I watched the old power move beneath the surface and waited for him to decide what kind of man he wanted to be in front of me.

I did not wait passively. I moved the chair into the circle and asked him to sit before refilling cups. Iroh had been trained to notice what people needed before they said it. I wanted to be more difficult than that. I wanted to say what I needed aloud and let him answer as a partner rather than a teacher. His gaze softened when I did. Not with pity. With recognition. There was a difference, and I was beginning to trust it.

We returned to the corner table where we first spoke. Iroh told the story in pieces, allowing ordinary details to matter. He remembered the light, the tea, and the foolish thing someone had said. He did not use wisdom to smooth every rough edge. Some memories were still sharp. I reached for his hand only after asking. He turned it over and threaded his fingers through mine. The gesture was small. The trust inside it was not.

“There is no honor in making yourself the only tired person.” Iroh said.

The work continued around us. We moved through wood grain, shared dishes, and who is allowed to rest as though the objects had been waiting for our conversation to finish. Iroh could make a room deliberate by changing a chair's angle. He could make a meal memorable by adding one spice. He could also forget to sit. I put a cup in front of him and called it an order. He bowed. “At last,” he said, “someone recognizes my need for supervision.”

I told him what I saw when he was not performing wisdom. He accepted being served without turning it into a lesson. Iroh had lost a son, a nation he once believed in, a throne he never wanted, and years to a war that taught the wrong definition of strength. He rebuilt himself through tea, laughter, food, music, and the decision to help one frightened nephew become better. I did not want to replace any of that. I wanted to be welcomed into the life after it.

I offered him a bite from my bowl. He took it with a smile and saved the last piece for me.

At the table, I let him be served without turning it into a lesson.

We left the empty chair in the circle. In the morning, there would be room for whoever needed a place, and room for us to sit down too. Iroh asked if I wanted to stay; I said yes. We let the rest of the night belong to us. Iroh asked if I wanted to stay; I said yes. We let the rest of the night belong to us.
